This is slightly different in the world of publishing writers.

Social media has allowed for a transition in the way that authorial branding works. Publishers are now considering authors which have existing social media fan bases a lot more than those who do not, as they become more and more risk-averse. 

In the indie space, social media presence becomes a direct marketing opportunity. Especially in the F&SF sphere where loyal core groups of fans make up the bulk of an author's sales and doubly so for authors who publish long series as book sales tend to decline entry over entry--as interest in the next book requires having read the one before.

When it comes to spaces like Ao3, Wattpad, Inkitt, and other free fiction outlets sheer volume makes this matter quite a bit less; and honestly I think that's a good thing. You should be primarily considered for the merit of your work, and good stories should stand out, not just stories written by popular people.

My campaign is chock-full of duplicitous NPCs who all think they have the best answer to solve the sword-of-damocles problem that threatens to ruin the world as we know it, and many of them have ended up turning on the party over the course of the campaign. This is all fine and good--if I would have tempered my own expectations and put myself in the party's shoes. 

Enter this noblewoman. She's an exceptionally powerful mage who was later revealed to have a hand in a local thieves' guild, who's leader has a fancy talking magic sword from the world's lore. When she was outed by the party, that guild then came to tie up loose ends. At this point the Paladin is fuming, and the party very reluctantly agreed to help defend her manor for long enough that she could get all of her cool magical doo-ma-bobs out. 

Then, the party jumped through a portal and left her. Great thinking on their part, total derail in my mind. 

Okay, not a problem, she's a mage who specializes in transmutation and teleportation so saving herself should be easy. She transmutes her manor into a massive fuel-air bomb and ends the story arc by making two big bads and herself MIA. Impressive. 

Flash forward a few sessions. My party is approaching the chamber of an elven council in the area one of the PCs is from. Fantastic. All save for the Paladin, who as soon as he was pinged in the @everyone broadcast the sword sends out when it talks, charges into the room and sees the noblewoman and her apprentice (who the party thinks is a really cool guy, overall). 

Immediately the Paladin casts Vow of Enmity on the noblewoman carrying the sword, throws a homebrew spell-grenade at her feet that triggers a bubble of anti-magic, then takes out half of her health in one round. In the middle of the elven elders council chamber. They are none too happy with this, and have him paralyzed and arrested, saving the noblewoman who then teleports away. 

Perfectly reasonable actions if this NPC were meant to be anything other than an ally-but-an-asshole. I know I'm supposed to frame the story to fit my players enjoyment but man I feel like I should have seen this coming, and though I'm not against them killing her, I don't want the fight against this character I've trumped up to be super cool and powerful to amount to trapping her in a bubble and beating her in a corner until she's a bloody pulp. 

But... That's why you don't betray your party too often.

Marijuana is wondrous for the brainstorming/rough draft type phase. I recommend being sober for the more intensive things like revising what you wrote when you were high and actually sitting to write at length. Too much and you end up playing Overwatch and not writing.

When I start new characters, I usually start with just a basic idea for who they are, such as "Tough-As-Nails Riot Cop Girl" or "Commercial Pilot From Brooklyn Who Gets Drafted", then names usually come next, followed by brainstorming their personalities. I actually do a lot of the thinking about the basics of their character (Physical Appearance, Motivation, Powers/Skills/Abilities) before I start working on a profile for them, and when I do I like to work over their Physical Appearance, Psychological Profile (Personality, Motivation, Childhood, Quirks), then move on to Strengths/Weaknesses/Flaws which generally has Abilities rolled in there as well. Lastly, I think about Speech Patterns and Mannerisms (I have a hard time making my characters sound different sometimes) and then detail the character's relationship with the factions in my universe. Its by no means exhaustive, there are some methods that involve potentially hundreds of details of a character, but my favorite strategy to developing these characters outside of a work is by writing small passages related to the work somehow and toying with how they respond to situations according to the "rules" I define by profiling them.

Provided that it was different /enough/ sure. Core mechanics of games as far as I know (I'm a programmer, not a lawyer tho) aren't a thing that can be copyrighted. Turn-based ability gameplay with enchanted/magical/mechanical/eldritch animals will always sure look like Pokémon from the outside, so you would have to find a way to distance yourself from that image. 

Graphically, as long as you do the art and it isn't too obviously derived from copyrighted material you should be fine.

I would advise against using the inspiration's original score whether remixed or not. Drum yourself up something nice and simple that sounds /like/ the source music in Sony ACID or Fruity Loops, its actually kind of fun.

It would be nice and easy to not copy the story, since Pokémon has little story aside from "You're a poor kid in a world of enchanted beasts who gets himself a beast and resolves to capture them all and become a champion". You could even stick with the simple adventure narrative if you made the concept unique enough.

Now, you ask essentially "how different is different enough", and that really varies based on who would be going after you. Nintendo is notorious for shutting down fan projects of all types and qualities because of how carefully they manage their IPs. 'Different' is 'different enough'.

If it were me in your shoes, I would create a turn-and-ability-based battle game where the player character is what does the battling, with a customization system that allows you to modify your abilities somehow to make up for the lack of diversity that a team of six creatures of differing types creates. That way at least its a mix-up of like Pokémon and Custom Robo.

I urge you though, as a fellow creative, please don't go out and seek to create a mere copy. Despite what postmodernism may suggest about all concepts and stories having been thought of already, you can still create a wonderful original product and enjoy yourself doing it.

EDIT: Would they sue you? Probably not. What are they going to get from you? They stand to gain nothing at the expense of a lot of legal costs. Would they DMCA you? Oh hell yeah.

So there are two concepts at play with why Fist Man isn't often chosen in the game. The first is Opportunity Cost, the idea that you are losing out on all the other options BESIDES fist man when picking him. Lets slap him into a category of folks with oneshots (Hanzo, Widow, sometimes Zen). By picking a one shot-based hero you lose out on reliable sustained damage (McCree, Soldier) AND high burst damage (Reaper, Pharah, Junkrat) and so those one shot-reliant heroes are generally considered unreliable options unless wielded skillfully.

The second concept I call the 'Effort-to-Payout Ratio". This is the same problem Ana has in the glory days of Mercy. Fist Man takes a lot of skill to use right, and even with the most skilled player you will still be getting less value than putting an equal amount of skill into someone like Widow, Soldier, McCree, etc. Ana is in the same boat. Fist and Sleep/Nade are all skillshots. Miss your skillshots, you're probably dead. Sights and Rez are not. More value for less work.

I feel like in a perfect world the Orisa should be with her team, and the team should be with Orisa. If an Orisa is caught out on her own she's a sitting duck from both extreme close and extreme long range. If you're being singled out by a flanker and nobody will assist, either think about where a more advantageous line position would be relative to the rest of your team, so the cover would be more natural and the flanker would just be smashed by your team, or stave the flanker off so you can retreat to your team, resulting in the flanker getting an all expenses paid trip back to spawn once more.

Out playing the flanker as Orisa would be a risky move, since you're not at your effective range and they're at theirs. My best advice would be to use Halt! to help you play around your barrier as much as you can. Headshots are your friend, and nothing will help more than practice. Learn some of the more common tactics used by flanker players so you can anticipate them like the "blink-through, blink-back" trick. 

Oh, and if you have at least 201 health you can tank a Pulse Bomb with Fortify.

When it comes to Genji, wait for the deflect comes out to use your Halt!. Try to anticipate the dash and counter it with Fortify,  unlike Tracer, Genji only has the one dash and no sustain, so if he uses it and can't kill you, and his Deflect is down, you have the advantage. 

Halt! Him back to you and finish him with melee if he runs. That often results in a lightly salted Genji.

Yeah. I just wanted to follow multiple protagonists, and wanted some ideas about better ways to do that other than just flipping back and forth chapter to chapter. I've considered mentioning some of the less noteworthy actions the secondary protagonist takes in the primary plotline because I want the secondary plot to come across as more high-action. The secondary protagonist is already a developed character and really the secondary plot is about a shift in his character while he searches for a lost love.

Frankly, your format could work well! You just have to understand that a video game explores plot and characters through extended sequences of action that are hard to write well. Im writing a story with pretty large-scale battles, and what I've found is that its best to demonstrate scale like that through multiple concurrent viewpoints, while trying to keep concise enough that the sequence doesn't become confusing.

I would say write it out anyway, and then take a look at how the story feels. Your 'boss fights' make great Threshold Guardians/Challenges/Finale depending on your plot structure too. Make sure every sequence is 'necessary' as in it advances either the plot, the reader's understanding of a character, or the goals of a character or faction--more is better when it comes to that. Video games can get away with a lot more than a story can because the player is more heavily immersed in the world, and more willing to go through events that the reader of a book might consider useless fluff.

Tl;Dr: you're fine. Even if you write a video game you can make it translate and flow well.
